Notes for [Workshop 3](https://mb5370.bioinformatics.guide/workshop3.html). Run the commands for this workshop in the Terminal, from inside the folder named under each heading. Copy each command you run into a bash chunk.

R chunks in this file run from the top of the repository, so give file paths from there, e.g. `flye_metagenome/mock/assembly_info.txt`.

## Step 1: Examine reads

Reads are linked into `raw_data/`.

```{bash}
# Start by making a symbolic link to the raw reads file in the raw_data folder.
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/raw_data
ln -s /pvol/data/metagenome_assembly/reads_R10_0.5.fastq.gz raw_reads.fastq.gz

# back “up” out of raw_data
cd ..

# check that the link is correct
ls -l raw_data

# Read length distribution
zcat raw_data/raw_reads.fastq.gz | head -n 40000 | bioawk -c fastx '{print $name,length($seq)}' > read_lengths.txt
```

Visualise read lengths in R in

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

rl_data <- read_tsv("read_lengths.txt",col_names = c("id","length"), show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(rl_data, aes(x=length/1000)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  xlab("Read Length Kb") + ylab("Number of Reads")
```

**Figure 1**: Histogram of read lengths in the mock nanopore sequencing dataset

Calculating read N50 (most reads are between 1 and 50kb in length).

- Step 1: Rank all reads from longest to shortest

- Step 2: Create a new column with the cumulative sum of read lengths (starting from longest read).

- Step 3: Find the read at which the cumulative sum surpasses 50% of the total read volume (ie total sum of all read lengths)

```{r}
total_len <- sum(rl_data$length)

rl_data |> 
  arrange(desc(length)) |> 
  mutate(cumsum = cumsum(length)) |> 
  filter(cumsum>total_len/2) |> 
  head(n=1)
```

Shows that N50 of the individual reads is about 22Kb.

## Step 2: Assembly

Commands run in `flye_metagenome/`.

Use flye for long-read metagenome data (use slurm job).

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/flye_metagenome
```

Create shell script and enter:

```{bash}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --time=360
#SBATCH --ntasks=4 --mem=6gb

echo "Starting flye in $(pwd) at $(date)"

flye --nano-hq ../raw_data/raw_reads.fastq.gz --threads 4 --out-dir mock --meta

echo "Finished flye in $(pwd) at $(date)"
```

Run shell script:

```{bash}
sbatch run_flye.sh
```

Monitor job output:

```{bash}
tail -f slurm-386.out
```

#### **Chromosome lengths and GC content in the reference data**

While I wait, I can compare the assembled contigs with reference genomes from the 5 species that comprise our mock community.

Create a new plain text file and add:

```{bash}
# Bioawk script for calculating gc and printing name,length,GC
BEGIN {
    OFS="\t"
}

{
    l=length($seq)
    ngc=gsub("[cgCG]","",$seq)
    nat=gsub("[taTA]","",$seq)
    print $name,l,ngc/(ngc+nat)
}
```

Look at reference genomes for mock community:

```{bash}
ls /pvol/data/mg/refs/*.fna
```

use `cat` to concatenate all the files together and then use a pipe to send their contents to our bioawk program. Run this from the top level of your project, where you saved `gc.awk`

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops
cat /pvol/data/mg/refs/*.fna | bioawk -c fastx -f gc.awk
```

## Step 3: Basic assembly QC

Commands run in `assembly_check/`.

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/assembly_check
# Use your gc.awk script to print GC and lengths for the assembly
cat ../flye_metagenome/mock/assembly.fasta | bioawk -c fastx -f ../gc.awk
# Run the command again but this time send outputs to a file called assembly.gc.tsv
cat ../flye_metagenome/mock/assembly.fasta | bioawk -c fastx -f ../gc.awk > assembly.gc.tsv
```

We have GC content in `assembly.gc.tsv` and coverage depth in the `assembly_info.txt` file produced by `flye`. Let’s read those and join them together using R.

```{r}
gc <- read_tsv("assembly_check/assembly.gc.tsv",col_names = c("#seq_name","length","GC"))
info <- read_tsv("flye_metagenome/mock/assembly_info.txt")
```

```{r}
# Since both datasets have a #seq_name column we can join them easily as follows:
gc_info <- info |> 
  left_join(gc)

gc_info |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=GC)) + geom_histogram() + ylab("Number of contigs")
```

**Figure 2**: Histogram of GC content values for assembled contigs in a flye assembly of the mock community dataset.

A histogram by GC content shows several peaks, probably corresponding to major groupings of taxonomically distinct lineages within the data.

```{r}
gc_info |> 
  filter(GC<0.8) |> 
  filter(cov.<25) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=GC,y=cov.)) + geom_point(aes(size=length)) + ylab("Coverage depth")
```

**Figure 3**: Coverage and GC content of assembled contigs in the mock community assembly. Contig lengths are shown through point size.

```{r}
library(ggrepel)
gc_info |> 
  filter(GC<0.8) |> 
  filter(cov.<25) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=GC,y=cov.)) + geom_point(aes(size=length)) + geom_label_repel(aes(label=`#seq_name`))
```

**Figure 4**: Coverage and GC content of assembled contigs in the mock community assembly. Contig lengths are shown through point size. Only contigs with less than 25x coverage and less than 80% GC content are shown.

#### **Assembly size vs reference size**

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops
# Firstly lets calculate the total length of our reference sequences. 
cat /pvol/data/mg/refs/*.fna | bioawk -c fastx -f gc.awk | awk '{sum+=$2}END{print sum}'
```

Calculate the total length of your assembly using R by taking the sum of the contig lengths column.

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops

cat /pvol/data/mg/refs/*.fna | bioawk -c fastx -f gc.awk | awk '{sum+=$2}END{print sum}'
```

```{r}
# total length of the Flye assembly in base pairs (bp).
total_assembly_length <- sum(gc_info$length)

total_assembly_length
```

## Step 4: Binning

Commands run in `metabat/`.

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/metabat
# Prepare an input file summarising read depth information for all contigs
cat ../flye_metagenome/mock/assembly_info.txt  | grep -v '#' | awk '{OFS="\t";print $1,$3}' > depths.txt

cat depths.txt | awk '{print $1}' | xargs samtools faidx ../flye_metagenome/mock/assembly.fasta > assembly_ordered.fasta

# Run metabat
metabat2 -i assembly_ordered.fasta -a depths.txt --cvExt -o bins/metabat --seed 5

# Inspect
grep '>' bins/*
```

## Step 5: Bin quality with CheckM

Commands run in `checkm/`.

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/checkm
# Firstly we prepare inputs for checkM. We copy the bins from metabat into the bins folder inside checkm
cp ../metabat/bins/metabat.*.fa bins/
```

Longest is contig_42

```{bash}
samtools faidx ../flye_metagenome/mock/assembly.fasta contig_42 > bins/contig_39.fa
```

Create shell file with:

`#!/bin/bash #SBATCH --time=60 #SBATCH --ntasks=4 --mem=40gb`

`echo "Starting checkm in $(pwd) at $(date)"`

`shopt -s expand_aliases alias checkm='apptainer run -B /pvol/:/pvol /pvol/data/sif/checkm.sif checkm'`

`checkm lineage_wf bins out -t 4 -x fa -f checkm_results.txt`

`echo "Finished checkm in $(pwd) at $(date)"`

```{bash}
sbatch run_checkm.sh

tail -f slurm-441.out
```

The checkm results:

metabat.7 shows strain heterogeneity (31.25%). It has 99.66% completeness, only 0.62% contamination; lineage is Vibrionaceae. Some duplicate marker genes are likely derived from closely related strains of the same organism rather than entirely different species.
